lessons.title: What's wrong?
lessons.goal: Say what hurts and how you feel.

tip.title: me duele la cabeza
tip.body: Doler (to hurt) works like gustar: the part that hurts is the subject. One thing: me duele la cabeza (my head hurts). Two or more: me duelen los pies (my feet hurt). Use el / la / los, not "my": me duele la espalda. To say how you feel in general: No me siento bien (I don't feel well). A friend will ask ¿Qué te pasa? (What's wrong?) and say ¡Que te mejores! (Get well soon!).

phrases.note: Mexico, informal: me duele la panza.

lines.name: Sofía
lines.t: Oye, ¿qué te pasa? Tienes mala cara.
lines.n: Hey, what's wrong? You don't look well.

lines.t: No me siento bien. Me duele mucho la cabeza.
lines.n: I don't feel well. My head really hurts.

lines.name: Sofía
lines.t: ¡Ay, pobre! ¿Te duele algo más?
lines.n: Oh, poor you! Does anything else hurt?

lines.t: Sí, también me duele la garganta.
lines.n: Yes, my throat hurts too.

lines.name: Sofía
lines.t: ¿Por qué no te vas a casa a descansar?
lines.n: Why don't you go home and rest?

lines.t: Tienes razón. Me voy a casa. ¡Gracias, Sofía!
lines.n: You're right. I'm going home. Thanks, Sofía!

lessons.title: At the doctor's
lessons.goal: Describe your symptoms and say since when.

tip.title: tengo fiebre, tengo tos
tip.body: Many symptoms use tener + a noun: tengo fiebre (I've got a temperature), tengo tos (I've got a cough), tengo gripe (I've got flu), tengo un resfriado (I've got a cold). Some use estar: estoy mareado / mareada (I feel dizzy). The doctor will use usted: ¿Desde cuándo tiene fiebre? Answer with desde hace + time: desde hace tres días (for three days), or desde + a point in time: desde ayer (since yesterday).

phrases.note: Spain also: tengo catarro. Mexico, colloquial: tengo gripa.

phrases.n: How long have you had a temperature?
Are you allergic to any medicine?

phrases.t: Le voy a recetar un jarabe.
phrases.n: I'm going to prescribe you a syrup.

dialogue.title: Doctora Ruiz, health centre in Valencia

lines.name: Doctora Ruiz
lines.t: Buenos días. Siéntese, por favor. ¿Qué le pasa?
lines.n: Good morning. Please sit down. What's the matter?

lines.t: Buenos días, doctora. Tengo fiebre y mucha tos.
lines.n: Good morning, doctor. I've got a temperature and a bad cough.

lines.name: Doctora Ruiz
lines.t: ¿Desde cuándo tiene fiebre?
lines.n: How long have you had a temperature?

lines.t: Desde hace tres días. Y también me duele la garganta.
lines.n: For three days. And my throat hurts too.

lines.name: Doctora Ruiz
lines.t: A ver… Es una gripe. ¿Tiene alergia a algún medicamento?
lines.n: Let's see… It's flu. Are you allergic to any medicine?

lines.t: No, a ninguno. ¿Tengo que tomar algo?
lines.n: No, none. Do I have to take anything?

prompts.n: Tell the doctor you've got a temperature and a cough.

lessons.title: At the pharmacy
lessons.goal: Ask for something for your symptoms and how to take it.

tip.title: ¿Tiene algo para…?
tip.body: The easiest way to ask at a pharmacy: ¿Tiene algo para la tos? (Have you got something for a cough?) or ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza? Las pastillas are tablets, el jarabe is syrup, la crema is cream, and la receta is the prescription. Ask how to take it with ¿Cuántas veces al día? (How many times a day?). Typical answer: una pastilla cada ocho horas (one tablet every eight hours).

phrases.n: Have you got something for a cough?

phrases.t: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?
phrases.n: Have you got something for a headache?

phrases.t: Necesito unas pastillas para la garganta.
Tome este jarabe después de comer.

lines.name: Farmacéutico
lines.t: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué se le ofrece?
lines.n: Good afternoon. What can I get you?

lines.t: Buenas tardes. ¿Tiene algo para la tos?
lines.n: Good afternoon. Have you got something for a cough?

lines.name: Farmacéutico
lines.t: Sí, este jarabe es muy bueno. ¿Tiene fiebre también?
lines.n: Yes, this syrup is very good. Have you got a temperature too?

lines.t: No, solo tos. ¿Necesito receta?
lines.n: No, just a cough. Do I need a prescription?

lines.name: Farmacéutico
lines.t: No, no necesita receta. Tome una cucharada cada ocho horas, después de comer.
lines.n: No, you don't need a prescription. Take a spoonful every eight hours, after meals.

lines.t: Muy bien, muchas gracias. ¿Cuánto es?
lines.n: Great, thanks a lot. How much is it?

prompts.n: Ask if they have something for a cough.
Ask if you need a prescription.
Ask how many times a day.

lessons.title: doler, tener que & hay que
lessons.goal: Say what hurts for anyone, and what someone has to do.

tip.title: me duele like me gusta; tengo que vs hay que
tip.body: Doler follows the gustar pattern: me duele, te duele, le duele, nos duele, les duele. The thing that hurts decides the ending: le duele la mano, le duelen las manos. With a name, add a: A mi madre le duele la rodilla. Tener que + infinitive is a personal obligation: tengo que descansar, tienes que ir al médico. Hay que + infinitive is a general rule ("you have to", "one must"): hay que beber mucha agua. Hay que never changes.

phrases.t: A mi hijo le duelen los oídos.
phrases.note: oídos = inner ears; orejas = the outer ears.

phrases.t: Tengo que tomar una pastilla cada ocho horas.
phrases.n: I have to take a tablet every eight hours.
You need to drink lots of water.

items.t: A mi madre le duele la cabeza.

base.n: I have to go to the doctor's.

items.n: You have to go to the doctor's.
You have to go to the doctor's. (polite)
You need to go to the doctor's. (general)

prompts.n: Tell a friend they have to rest.

t: A mi hijo le duelen los oídos
A mi hijo le duele el oído

lessons.title: A fall in the park
lessons.goal: Follow a story about an accident and the doctor's advice.

story.title: Dani's crutches
story.intro: Inés visits her friend Dani in Bilbao and finds him on crutches.

lines.name: Inés
lines.t: ¡Dani! ¿Qué te ha pasado? ¿Por qué llevas muletas?
lines.n: Dani! What's happened to you? Why are you on crutches?

lines.name: Dani
lines.t: Ayer me caí de la bici en el parque. ¡Me duele todo!
lines.n: Yesterday I fell off my bike in the park. Everything hurts!

lines.name: Inés
lines.t: ¡Ay, pobre! ¿Fuiste al médico?
lines.n: Oh, poor you! Did you go to the doctor?

lines.name: Dani
lines.t: Sí, fui a urgencias. Me hicieron una radiografía del pie.
lines.n: Yes, I went to A&E. They X-rayed my foot.

lines.name: Inés
lines.t: ¿Y está roto?
lines.n: And is it broken?

lines.name: Dani
lines.t: No, menos mal. Es un esguince, pero tengo que llevar muletas dos semanas.
lines.n: No, thank goodness. It's a sprain, but I have to use crutches for two weeks.

lines.name: Inés
lines.t: ¿Y qué más te ha dicho el médico?
lines.n: And what else did the doctor tell you?

lines.name: Dani
lines.t: Tengo que descansar y no puedo caminar mucho. Hay que poner hielo tres veces al día. ¡Y nada de fútbol!
lines.n: I have to rest and I can't walk much. I need to put ice on it three times a day. And no football!

questions.q: ¿Cuántas veces al día tiene que poner hielo?
questions.n: How many times a day does he have to put ice on?

lessons.title: Booking a doctor's appointment
lessons.goal: Phone a doctor's office and get an appointment.

phrases.n: I'd like to make an appointment.

phrases.t: Me duele la garganta desde hace dos días.
phrases.n: My throat has hurt for two days.

phrases.note: Spain: Mi número de móvil es…

branch.title: On the phone to the consultorio
branch.scene: You've been ill for two days in Guadalajara, Mexico. You call a doctor's private office (consultorio) to get an appointment.
branch.name: Recepcionista

choices.n: Good morning. I'd like to make an appointment, please.

busy.n: The doctor is with a patient. Would you like to make an appointment?

choices.t: Sí, por favor. Necesito una cita.

when.n: You can come today at six in the evening or tomorrow at ten. Which suits you better?

choices.t: Hoy a las seis, por favor.
Mañana a las diez está bien.

name.t: Perfecto. ¿Me da su nombre y un número de teléfono?
name.n: Perfect. Can you give me your name and a phone number?

lessons.title: Explaining your symptoms
lessons.goal: Describe your symptoms to a doctor for 45 seconds.

culture.title: The pharmacy: your first stop
culture.body: In Spain you'll recognise a pharmacy by its green cross, often lit up at night. Spanish pharmacists are trained health professionals, and many people ask them for advice on minor problems before going to the doctor. Medicines are sold only in pharmacies, and every area has a farmacia de guardia that stays open at night and on holidays: the other pharmacies post its address on their door. In Mexico, many pharmacies have a small doctor's office (consultorio) next door, where you can see a doctor quickly for a low fee. In both countries, antibiotics need a prescription.

phrases.note: Common in Spain. Everywhere: me siento mal.

phrases.t: Hay un consultorio al lado de la farmacia.
phrases.n: There's a doctor's office next to the pharmacy.

free.n: You're at the doctor's. Explain what's wrong: what hurts, your symptoms, since when, and ask what you have to do.
